title: Warm season variability and aquatic biodiversity assessment in the lower Los Angeles River (CA, USA) using environmental DNA
content:
Abstract
Urban ecology examines how biodiversity and ecological processes persist in human-modified environments. The Los Angeles River has been transformed by urbanization into a concrete flood control channel with altered flow regimes, degraded water quality, and reduced habitat quality. We used this site to assess how seasonal environmental variation influences aquatic biodiversity in a highly urbanized river. Monthly environmental DNA samples and corresponding water quality data were collected at two sites along the lower Los Angeles River over a six-month period spanning warm and cool seasons. Water quality parameters tested in this study included temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, oxidation-reduction potential, and inorganic constituents such as nitrate and sulfate. Metabarcoding of environmental DNA samples were done using cytochrome oxidase I primers and processed with the Anacapa Toolkit for taxonomic classification. Results revealed a shift in relative dominance from arthropods in summer to diatoms in fall. Stress-tolerant taxa such as Tubificidae, ostracods, and oligochaetes persisted under warm, low-oxygen conditions, while sensitive taxa like Baetidae (mayflies) were more abundant during cooler periods with elevated dissolved oxygen. The co-occurrence of tolerant and sensitive groups suggests a transitional ecosystem shaped by fluctuating stressors and the heterogeneous nature of urban stream ecosystems. We found that environmental DNA effectively captured seasonal shifts in community structure and provides a valuable tool for monitoring biodiversity in response to environmental change. This work supports ongoing efforts to evaluate restoration outcomes and improve ecological conditions in urban rivers like the Los Angeles River.
